bill.name: Proposing an amendment to the Constitution of the United States relating to the authority of Congress and the States to regulate contributions and expenditures intended to affect elections and to enact public financing systems for political campaigns (H.J. Res. 122)
bill.status: Introduced in House · Rep. Joe Neguse · referred to House Judiciary on September 17, 2025
bill.analyzed: Full introduced joint resolution: proposed article, numbered clauses 1–4, and ratification condition

sourceLimits: The supplied 2,865-byte, 457-word raw source is a flattened extraction of the introduced-in-House joint resolution. It has no page boundaries or metadata sidecar, and it omits the standard resolving formula—including the two-thirds-of-each-House concurrence language—visible in the separately checked official PDF; that PDF establishes the three-page count. The text proposes ratification-contingent constitutional authority, not a campaign-finance rule or public-financing program. It sets no contribution or expenditure limit, creates no financing system or artificial-entity prohibition, appropriates no public funding, assigns no administrator, requires no report, supplies no baseline, and states no measurable downstream outcome. The proposed article itself supplies none of those concrete measures; any new rules, programs, prohibitions, or appropriations would require later Federal or State action, while effects on existing law are outside the supplied text. Campaign-finance totals would not by themselves measure the stated influence of private wealth, viewpoint neutrality, or effects on freedom of the press. The number of ratifying legislatures, including whether three-fourths ratify on time, is an objectively resolvable one-time legal milestone rather than a recurring policy-outcome series. At the introduced stage there is no submission date and therefore no fixed seven-year deadline, and the text creates no named resolver or recurring official data product. This extraction keeps that adoption gate in context and barriers rather than promoting it into the outcome-metric scope. Accordingly, it has one provision and four text-grounded goals, but zero recurring, downstream, or registry-ready outcome metrics; metrics, stance matrices, series hints, and empirical conditionals are empty.

provisions.title: Proposed constitutional article — Clauses 1–4
provisions.heading: Campaign-finance authority, public financing, entity distinctions, and press safeguard
provisions.quote: “Congress and the States may regulate and impose reasonable viewpoint-neutral limitations on the raising and spending of money by candidates and others to influence elections.” … “Nothing in this article shall be construed to grant Congress or the States the power to abridge the freedom of the press.”
provisions.context: H.J. Res. 122 proposes one constitutional article rather than an ordinary statutory program. The resolving formula in the separately checked official PDF, omitted from the supplied raw extraction, requires two-thirds of each House to concur before submission. After submission, the article becomes valid only if the legislatures of three-fourths of the States ratify it within seven years. Clause 1 permits reasonable viewpoint-neutral limits on election-related raising and spending; Clause 2 permits public campaign-financing systems; Clause 3 supplies implementation and enforcement power and permits distinctions between natural persons and artificial entities; and Clause 4 says the article grants no power to abridge freedom of the press. These are grants of authority rather than the contents of a concrete regulatory regime: the proposed article itself sets no numeric limit, establishes no financing system, prohibits no entity's spending, and spends no public money.
goals: Give Congress and the States authority to impose reasonable viewpoint-neutral limits on raising and spending money to influence elections.
Give Congress and the States authority to enact public campaign-financing systems, including systems designed to restrict private-wealth influence through increased public funding.

Give Congress and the States power to implement and enforce the article through legislation and to distinguish natural persons from artificial entities, including by prohibiting artificial-entity election spending.
Prevent the article's grant of authority from being construed as a power to abridge freedom of the press.

effects.text: The proposed article would have no constitutional effect unless three-fourths of the State legislatures ratify it within seven years after its submission for ratification.

If ratified, the article would establish constitutional powers and constraints, but it does not specify a concrete contribution rule, expenditure rule, or enforcement regime, or state how existing laws would be affected.

effects.mechanism: Public financing remains a later policy choice
effects.text: Clause 2 would authorize public campaign-financing systems, including offsetting designs, but it creates no program, eligibility rule, payment formula, funding source, or appropriation.

effects.mechanism: Entity distinction bounded by the press safeguard
effects.text: Clause 3 would permit different treatment of natural persons and artificial entities, including a prohibition on artificial-entity election spending, while Clause 4 withholds any newly granted power to abridge freedom of the press; the text does not resolve every boundary between those clauses.

barriers.text: The analyzed version is introduced and referred, not submitted for ratification; the official resolving formula requires two-thirds of each House to concur before submission, after which three-fourths of State legislatures must ratify before the seven-year deadline.

Ratification would authorize rather than compel action, so any new limit, financing system, entity rule, administrative arrangement, or public-funding amount would require later policy choices and, where money is spent, funding authority.
The text supplies no decision rules for “reasonable,” “viewpoint-neutral,” “to influence elections,” or the boundary between artificial-entity regulation and freedom of the press.
